lead: Abraham walks with his three visitors towards Sodom, and the Lord shares his plan with him. Abraham then dares to intercede: will the Judge of all the earth sweep away the righteous with the wicked? From fifty down to ten, God agrees to spare the city. In the Gospel Jesus tells a would-be follower that the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head, and tells another, “Follow me.” Psalm 103 sings of the Lord who is kind and merciful. Today the Church keeps the memorial of St Irenaeus, bishop and Doctor of the Church.

r.h: Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?
set: The visitors who promised Isaac now look toward Sodom, the city of the plain whose sin had become notorious (13:13). God decides to share his purpose with Abraham, because Abraham is to teach his children “righteousness and justice”. What follows is the first great prayer of intercession in the Bible.

Scripture describes the sin of Sodom in more than one way: the violence and abuse against guests in chapter 19, and, in Ezekiel 16:49, pride, excess of food and prosperous ease, and failing to help the poor and needy.
str: vv. 16–19: God decides not to hide his plan from Abraham, chosen to teach justice.
vv. 20–21: the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah.
vv. 22–25: Abraham stands before the Lord: “Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?”
vv. 26–32: from fifty to forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, ten; each time God agrees.
v. 33: the Lord goes his way; Abraham returns home.
kw: The cry of the oppressed for help, the same kind of cry as Israel’s in Egypt (Exodus 3:7–9). God hears the voice of the victims.
One who is right with God and with neighbour. Abraham’s question is whether the presence of a few righteous people can save a whole city.
Abraham knows how small he is before God (v. 27), yet he speaks. Humility and boldness go together in true prayer.
vv: Shall I hide from Abraham what I am about to do,
God treats Abraham as a friend, sharing his counsel with him. Later Scripture calls Abraham the friend of God (Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23).
Will you indeed sweep away the righteous with the wicked?
Abraham appeals to God’s own justice. He is not arguing against God but holding God to what God is.
Shall not the Judge of all the earth do what is just?
The key question of the chapter. God is the judge not only of Israel but of all nations, and his judgment is never unjust.
For the sake of ten I will not destroy it.
Abraham stops at ten, and the Lord would have spared the city for ten. The righteous few protect the many.
ch: The Catechism says that once God had confided his plan, Abraham’s heart was attuned to his Lord’s compassion for men, and he dared to intercede for them with bold confidence (CCC 2571). It adds that since Abraham, intercession, asking on behalf of another, has been characteristic of a heart attuned to God’s mercy (CCC 2635). The Church sees the fullness of this prayer in Christ, the one righteous man, for whose sake the many are spared, who “always lives to make intercession” for us (Hebrews 7:25).

set: Crowds press around Jesus, and he gives orders to cross the lake. Before he gets into the boat, two men speak to him about following. Matthew places these sayings just before the storm on the lake (8:23–27), where following Jesus will mean being in the boat with him in danger.
str: v. 18: Jesus gives orders to cross to the other side.
vv. 19–20: a scribe: “I will follow you wherever you go”; the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.
vv. 21–22: a disciple: “let me first bury my father”; “Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.”
kw: A teacher of the law. The scribe calls Jesus “Teacher” and offers to follow, with good will. Jesus wants him to know the cost.
Jesus’ favourite way of speaking of himself. Here it is used for the first time in Matthew, of his homelessness. The same title will be used of his suffering and of his coming in glory.
The word of discipleship. It appears in both scenes and again in v. 23, when the disciples follow him into the boat.
vv: Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.
A generous promise. Jesus does not refuse him, but makes sure he knows where Jesus goes.
Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.
The wild animals have more security than he does. To follow him is to share his poverty and his trust in the Father.
Follow me, and let the dead bury their own dead.

Burial of a father was among the most sacred duties in Jewish life. Jesus’ words are deliberately shocking, to show the urgency of the kingdom. Many Fathers and commentators take “the dead” to mean those who are spiritually dead, who have not yet heard the call.
ch: The Church does not read this Gospel as a rejection of care for parents, which the fourth commandment requires (CCC 2214–2220). She reads it as a call to put Christ first. The Catechism teaches that Jesus calls his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone (CCC 2544). Priests, religious and missionaries who leave home and family live this saying in a visible way; every Christian lives it when the call of Christ comes before comfort.

rite: St Irenaeus was born in Asia Minor, probably at Smyrna, between about 130 and 140. As a young man he heard St Polycarp, who had known the apostle John, so he stands very close to the apostles. He became a priest at Lyons in Gaul and, after the martyrdom of Bishop Pothinus in 177, its bishop. His great work, usually called Against Heresies, defended the faith against the Gnostic teachers by pointing to Scripture, the rule of faith and the succession of bishops from the apostles, above all in the Church of Rome, which he called founded and organised by the two most glorious apostles, Peter and Paul (Against Heresies 3.3.2); the Catechism quotes the same passage on the communion of all the Churches with Rome (CCC 834). He wrote that “the glory of God is man fully alive” (CCC 294), and that the knot of Eve’s disobedience was loosed by Mary’s obedience (CCC 494). He is honoured as a martyr, though the details of his death are not known. In 2022 Pope Francis declared him a Doctor of the Church, calling him the Doctor of Unity. Like Abraham, he spoke for the whole Church; like the disciples in the Gospel, he left his homeland to follow Christ.
study: Abraham prayed boldly for a city that was not his own. For which town, nation or people can I pray with the same persistence this week?
What “first let me…” do I put between myself and Christ’s call?
